questions.stem: The Geneva Accords of July 1954 described the line dividing Vietnam as:
options: a provisional military demarcation line, not a political or territorial boundary
a permanent international border between two separate and sovereign Vietnamese states
a ceasefire line to be patrolled by a United Nations peacekeeping force
the new frontier between French Indochina and the Viet Minh's republic
questions.explanation: The Accords followed the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954. They separated the forces at the 17th parallel as a temporary measure until nationwide elections, which were to be held in July 1956. The line was never meant to create two states.

questions.stem: What did the Geneva Conference of 1954 decide for Laos and Cambodia?
options: Both were absorbed into a federation led by the State of Vietnam
Both were recognised as independent, and foreign forces were to withdraw
Both were placed under a joint French and Chinese trusteeship for a further six years
Both were to hold referendums on joining either North or South Vietnam
questions.explanation: Laos and Cambodia were confirmed as independent states, and Viet Minh and French forces were to leave. In Laos the communist Pathet Lao were given two northern provinces to regroup in until they were integrated, which left a base for later conflict.

questions.stem: Which best describes US policy towards South Vietnam under President Eisenhower (1954-1961)?
options: withdrawing all aid once the last French troops left Indochina
funding and advising Diem's government and army to build a non-communist state
sending large US combat forces to fight the communist guerrillas in the southern provinces
pressing Diem to hold the 1956 nationwide elections on schedule
questions.explanation: The USA paid for much of South Vietnam's budget and army and sent a small group of military advisers. It also created SEATO in 1954, whose protocol covered South Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. US combat troops came only in 1965.

questions.stem: The nationwide elections planned at Geneva for 1956 were never held mainly because:
options: the United Nations cancelled them after fighting broke out in Laos
France postponed them until its last troops had left Vietnam
Diem refused to hold them, with US backing, expecting Ho Chi Minh to win
North Vietnam refused to hold them, expecting Diem's candidates to win in the south
questions.explanation: Diem argued that free elections were impossible in the communist North, and the USA, which believed Ho Chi Minh would win, supported him. The division at the 17th parallel therefore hardened into two rival states.

questions.stem: How did President Kennedy's policy towards Vietnam (1961-1963) differ from Eisenhower's?
options: He greatly increased the number of US advisers and backed counter-insurgency
He sent the first US ground combat divisions and began a bombing campaign against the North
He ended aid to Diem and opened talks with Hanoi on neutralising Vietnam
He handed responsibility for defending South Vietnam to SEATO's members
questions.explanation: US military advisers rose from under a thousand to about 16,000 by late 1963, with helicopter units and Special Forces. Kennedy favoured counter-insurgency rather than conventional war. Large combat forces and sustained bombing of the North began under Johnson in 1965.

questions.stem: The Strategic Hamlet Program of 1962 moved peasants into fortified villages to cut them off from the NLF. Why did it largely fail?
options: It worked well until 1962, when US combat troops replaced the ARVN as the hamlets' defenders
Peasants welcomed it, but the NLF had already moved its forces into the cities
Kennedy cancelled it before any hamlets had been built in the countryside
Forced relocation angered peasants, and many hamlets were infiltrated or poorly defended
questions.explanation: Peasants resented being moved from their land and ancestral graves and forced to build defences. Many hamlets were poorly protected, and NLF agents operated inside them. The program collapsed after Diem's overthrow in 1963.

questions.stem: Which feature of Ngo Dinh Diem's government most weakened its support in South Vietnam?
options: its refusal to accept any American aid or military advisers
favouritism towards Catholics and his family, and repression of opponents
radical land reform that took farms from Catholic landowners
a close alliance with the Buddhist clergy against the army
questions.explanation: Diem, a Catholic, relied on his family, especially his brother Ngo Dinh Nhu, and on Catholic officials in a mostly Buddhist country. The Buddhist crisis of 1963, which began when troops fired on protesters in Hue, turned many against him. Generals overthrew and killed him in November 1963, and unstable military governments followed.

questions.stem: In North Vietnam, the land reform campaign of 1953-1956:
options: returned confiscated land to the former landlords to win their support for the war
was cancelled before any land had changed hands because of peasant resistance
was run by French officials who stayed on in Hanoi after the Geneva Accords
redistributed land but caused abuses that the party later admitted were errors
questions.explanation: Land was taken from landlords and given to poor peasants, but the campaign used denunciation tribunals and many people were wrongly accused and executed. In 1956 the party launched a 'rectification of errors' and Ho Chi Minh publicly acknowledged its mistakes.

questions.stem: In 1959 the leaders of North Vietnam decided to:
options: accept the division of Vietnam and seek UN membership as a separate state
invade the South at once with conventional divisions, tanks and artillery
end support for southern communists in return for more Soviet aid
support armed struggle in the South and build a supply route through Laos
questions.explanation: Southern communists had suffered badly under Diem's repression. In 1959 the party approved a return to armed struggle and set up a unit to build the route through Laos that became the Ho Chi Minh Trail. The National Liberation Front followed in December 1960.

questions.stem: The National Liberation Front (NLF), formed in December 1960, was:
options: an alliance of ARVN officers secretly planning a coup against Diem
a US-trained village militia created to defend hamlets from guerrillas
a southern front aiming to overthrow Diem, directed by Hanoi's communist party
a Buddhist political party committed to nonviolent opposition to Diem
questions.explanation: The NLF presented itself as a broad southern nationalist front, but its leadership was controlled by the Vietnamese communist party in Hanoi. Its opponents called its fighters the Viet Cong, short for Vietnamese communists.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why Ho Chi Minh's movement won wide support among Vietnamese?
options: It joined communism to the nationalist cause of independence and unity
It promised to restore the Nguyen emperors and their Confucian traditions
It relied on Catholic villagers who had moved south from the north in 1954
It abandoned communism to win aid from the United States and Britain
questions.explanation: The Viet Minh, founded in 1941, led the fight against French rule and Japanese occupation, giving Ho great nationalist credibility. Communist land reform also appealed to poor peasants. Many Catholics, by contrast, moved south in 1954-1955 to escape communist rule.

questions.stem: A historian argues that US leaders misread the conflict as Soviet or Chinese expansion when it was mainly a war of national liberation. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: Ho Chi Minh had worked as an agent of the Comintern in the 1920s and 1930s
Hanoi pursued its own goals and resisted control by both Moscow and Beijing
North Vietnam relied heavily on Soviet and Chinese weapons throughout the war
The NLF in the South took its direction from the communist party in Hanoi
questions.explanation: Vietnam had a long history of resisting China, and Hanoi balanced between its two allies rather than obeying either. The other pieces of evidence show communist links, which support the US view of a Cold War struggle rather than challenge it.

questions.stem: Why do historians regard the second reported attack in the Gulf of Tonkin, on 4 August 1964, as significant?
options: It was ordered by Diem to force the USA to commit its combat troops
It almost certainly never happened, yet it was used to win broad war powers
It sank a US destroyer, causing the heaviest US naval losses of the whole war
It was carried out by China, drawing Beijing directly into the conflict
questions.explanation: North Vietnamese boats did attack the USS Maddox on 2 August, but later evidence shows the second attack did not occur. Johnson used the incidents to gain the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, which let him use force without a declaration of war. Diem had been dead since 1963.

questions.stem: Which pair of decisions in 1965 marked the Americanisation of the war?
options: Operation Linebacker and the mining of Haiphong harbour
the Strategic Hamlet Program and the arrival of the first advisers
the incursion into Cambodia and the policy of Vietnamization
Operation Rolling Thunder and the landing of US Marines at Da Nang
questions.explanation: Sustained bombing of North Vietnam began in March 1965, and the first US combat troops, Marines, landed at Da Nang that month. US forces grew to more than half a million by 1968. Linebacker and Vietnamization belong to the Nixon years.

questions.stem: Which tactic did NLF and North Vietnamese forces use to reduce the effect of US firepower?
options: pulling all their forces back into North Vietnam whenever US troops arrived
relying on their own air force to protect their units from US bombing raids
fighting at close quarters, so air and artillery strikes risked hitting US troops
fighting in open terrain where they could concentrate all their tanks and artillery
questions.explanation: Communist forces tried to 'hold the enemy by the belt', staying close so the USA could not use its air power and artillery freely. They also used ambushes, booby traps and tunnel systems such as those at Cu Chi, and chose when and where to fight.

questions.stem: Why was the Ho Chi Minh Trail so important to North Vietnam's strategy, and so hard for the USA to cut?
options: It was a single paved highway that North Vietnam guarded with its tanks and heavy artillery
It ran along the coast under the protection of the Soviet and Chinese navies
It crossed the demilitarised zone directly, where the USA had agreed not to fight
It carried men and supplies south through Laos and Cambodia, beyond US ground forces
questions.explanation: The trail was a network of tracks and roads through the jungles of eastern Laos and Cambodia. Heavy bombing slowed but never stopped it, because the routes were constantly repaired and changed and US ground troops did not operate in Laos.

questions.stem: How did North Vietnam manage its relations with China and the Soviet Union during the war?
options: It took aid from both while balancing between them during the Sino-Soviet split
It sided fully with China and refused all further Soviet aid after the split in 1960
It sided fully with the USSR and expelled every Chinese adviser in 1965
It refused aid from both to keep its independence from all foreign powers
questions.explanation: The USSR supplied surface-to-air missiles, jet fighters and heavy weapons, while China sent engineering and anti-aircraft troops, small arms and food. Hanoi avoided taking sides in the Sino-Soviet dispute so it could keep aid flowing from both.

questions.stem: China sent engineering and anti-aircraft troops to North Vietnam from 1965. How did this shape US strategy?
options: Fear of a war with China, as in Korea, ruled out a US invasion of the North
It led the USA to bomb Chinese cities in retaliation from the start of 1966
It forced North Vietnam to stop sending its own troops into the South
It ended the Sino-Soviet split and united the communist bloc against the USA
questions.explanation: US leaders remembered how China had entered the Korean War in 1950 when UN forces neared its border. They therefore limited the war to bombing the North and fighting in the South, which let Hanoi keep its base secure.

questions.stem: Which weakness of the Army of the Republic of Vietnam (ARVN) was most often reported by US advisers?
options: a refusal to accept any US weapons, training or advisers in its units
a policy of fighting only inside North Vietnam rather than defending the South
officers promoted for political loyalty, high desertion and reliance on US firepower
a shortage of soldiers, since it never had more than 50,000 men under arms
questions.explanation: The ARVN grew to around a million men, but many senior officers owed their posts to politics, and desertion was high. Some units fought well, as at An Loc in 1972, yet the army had been built to depend on American air power and supply.

questions.stem: The Tet Offensive began in late January 1968 with:
options: a guerrilla campaign limited to villages in the Mekong delta and the far south
an attack on US air bases in Thailand and Laos by North Vietnamese commandos
coordinated attacks on cities and towns across South Vietnam during a holiday truce
a conventional tank invasion of South Vietnam launched directly across the 17th parallel
questions.explanation: NLF and North Vietnamese forces struck more than a hundred towns and cities, including Saigon, where they briefly entered the US Embassy compound, and Hue, which they held for weeks. The attacks came during the Tet lunar new year holiday.

questions.stem: Militarily, the NLF suffered heavy losses in the Tet Offensive. Which outcome best shows why Tet was still a turning point?
options: Congress responded to the attack on Saigon by formally declaring war on the North
Johnson limited the bombing, offered talks and announced he would not seek re-election
The USA sent all the extra troops Westmoreland had requested and then invaded North Vietnam
Peasants across South Vietnam rose up in support of the NLF, as Hanoi had hoped
questions.explanation: Tet shattered official claims that the war was being won and widened the 'credibility gap'. On 31 March 1968 Johnson announced a partial bombing halt, offered negotiations and withdrew from the presidential race. The hoped-for popular uprising did not happen.

questions.stem: What happened at My Lai in March 1968?
options: NLF forces killed several hundred US soldiers in a night ambush
ARVN troops mutinied and handed their base over to the NLF
US aircraft mistakenly bombed a South Vietnamese army base
US soldiers killed several hundred unarmed Vietnamese villagers
questions.explanation: A US Army company killed several hundred unarmed civilians, mostly women, children and old men. The army covered it up until journalists revealed it in November 1969. Lieutenant William Calley was the only soldier convicted, and the case deepened opposition to the war.

questions.stem: Operation Ranch Hand (1962-1971) sprayed herbicides such as Agent Orange in order to:
options: strip forest cover and destroy crops that could feed enemy forces
clear the minefields laid around US bases and airfields in the South
kill the malaria-carrying mosquitoes found in the Mekong delta
poison the water supplies of cities in North Vietnam
questions.explanation: Millions of litres of herbicide destroyed forests, mangroves and farmland. Agent Orange was contaminated with dioxin, which has been linked to serious illness and birth defects. Bombing, napalm, free-fire zones and forced relocation also drove millions of villagers into refugee camps and cities.

questions.stem: The war in Laos is often called the 'Secret War' because:
options: no foreign forces of any kind fought in Laos at any time between 1962 and 1975
the Pathet Lao fought without the knowledge or support of North Vietnam
the 1962 Geneva agreement banned all journalists from entering the country
the CIA ran a covert campaign with Hmong forces and heavy bombing, hidden from the public
questions.explanation: The 1962 agreement made Laos neutral, so the USA hid its role. The CIA armed Hmong forces under General Vang Pao, and US aircraft bombed Laos from 1964 to 1973, making it one of the most heavily bombed countries per person in history. Unexploded bomblets went on killing civilians for decades.

questions.stem: How was Cambodia drawn into the war in 1969 and 1970?
options: Secret US bombing of sanctuaries, Lon Nol's coup, then a US and ARVN incursion
A Khmer Rouge invasion of South Vietnam in support of the NLF fighting in the Mekong delta
Sihanouk's request for US combat troops to defend the capital, Phnom Penh
A Chinese invasion of eastern Cambodia to protect the Ho Chi Minh Trail
questions.explanation: Sihanouk had tolerated North Vietnamese bases on the border. Secret US bombing began in March 1969, Lon Nol overthrew Sihanouk in March 1970, and US and ARVN forces entered Cambodia in April-May 1970. The fighting spread across the country.

questions.stem: Which best explains the growth of the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia between 1970 and 1975?
options: US support for the Khmer Rouge as a counterweight to North Vietnam's forces
a free election in 1972 that gave the Khmer Rouge a majority in parliament
Soviet troops who installed Pol Pot in Phnom Penh at the start of 1973
Sihanouk's backing after his overthrow, the war's destruction and Lon Nol's weak regime
questions.explanation: After his overthrow, Sihanouk allied with the Khmer Rouge, giving them peasant support. North Vietnamese help, a corrupt and failing Lon Nol government and the devastation of bombing and fighting all helped them grow. Historians debate how much the bombing itself added to recruitment.

questions.stem: After capturing Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975, the Khmer Rouge:
options: united Cambodia with Vietnam under the government in Hanoi
emptied the cities and forced the population into rural labour
held elections that returned Sihanouk to full executive power
invited US and Western aid to rebuild the capital's industries
questions.explanation: The Khmer Rouge marched city dwellers into the countryside to work in agricultural communes, abolished money and markets, and executed officials of the old regime. Huge numbers of people died from execution, starvation and overwork under their rule.

questions.stem: Which development best shows the US anti-war movement broadening beyond students by the late 1960s?
options: a vote by Congress in 1967 to cut off all funding for the war in Vietnam
Johnson's resignation from the presidency in 1968 under mass protests
Martin Luther King's opposition to the war and protests by Vietnam veterans
the abolition of the draft in 1965 after student demonstrations on campuses
questions.explanation: King spoke out against the war in 1967, and groups such as Vietnam Veterans Against the War gave protest added weight. Huge crowds joined the Moratorium of October 1969. The draft ended only in 1973, and Johnson finished his term after deciding not to run again.

questions.stem: In May 1970, National Guard troops shot dead four students at Kent State University in Ohio. What had sparked the protest?
options: the start of the first draft lottery since the Second World War
the publication of the Pentagon Papers in the New York Times
Nixon's announcement of US and ARVN operations in Cambodia
the first newspaper reports of the killings at My Lai
questions.explanation: Nixon announced the Cambodian incursion on 30 April 1970, and protests broke out on campuses across the USA. The Kent State shootings followed on 4 May, and hundreds of colleges were disrupted by strikes. My Lai was revealed in 1969 and the Pentagon Papers in 1971.

questions.stem: Historians debate the influence of the US anti-war movement. Which statement is best supported by the evidence?
options: It added to pressure for withdrawal, though many Americans also disliked protesters
It forced an immediate US withdrawal in 1968 against Johnson's own wishes
It had almost no support outside a small number of university campuses
It persuaded Congress to declare war so that the draft could be abolished
questions.explanation: Protest helped turn opinion and shaped decisions by Johnson and Nixon, yet polls showed many Americans opposed both the war and the protesters. Nixon appealed to what he called the 'silent majority' in 1969, and US troops did not leave until 1973.

questions.stem: President Nixon's policy of Vietnamization meant:
options: withdrawing US troops while training and arming the ARVN to take over the fighting
increasing the number of US troops until North Vietnam agreed to surrender
handing the defence of South Vietnam to a United Nations peacekeeping force
uniting Vietnam at once under a neutral coalition government led from Hanoi
questions.explanation: Under the Nixon Doctrine of 1969, allies were expected to provide their own ground forces. US troop numbers fell from over half a million in 1969 to fewer than 30,000 by the end of 1972, while US air power continued to support the ARVN.

questions.stem: The ARVN's 1971 operation into Laos, Lam Son 719, is often used to judge Vietnamization. Why?
options: Without US advisers on the ground, the ARVN suffered heavy losses and retreated
The ARVN destroyed the trail's main bases and ended the supply route for the rest of the war
US ground troops did all the fighting while the ARVN guarded the border
The ARVN refused to cross into Laos, so the operation had to be cancelled
questions.explanation: US law barred American ground troops from Laos, so the ARVN went in with only US air support. After fierce resistance it pulled back in disorder, suggesting it was not yet able to fight major battles alone.

questions.stem: Under the Paris Peace Accords signed in January 1973:
options: North Vietnam agreed to withdraw every one of its divisions from South Vietnam by the end of 1973
Vietnam was to be reunited at once under the Saigon government of Nguyen Van Thieu
the USA was allowed to keep 50,000 combat troops in the South as a guarantee
US forces would leave within 60 days, while North Vietnamese troops stayed in the South
questions.explanation: After the Christmas bombing of December 1972, the agreement was signed on 27 January 1973. It provided for a ceasefire, US withdrawal and the return of prisoners of war, but left North Vietnamese forces in place in the South. The last US combat troops left in March 1973.

questions.stem: Which best explains why the USA withdrew from Vietnam?
options: the ARVN had defeated the NLF, so US troops were no longer needed
the Soviet Union threatened nuclear war unless the USA withdrew
the United Nations ordered the USA to withdraw its forces in 1971
rising costs, opposition at home and an attrition strategy that had failed
questions.explanation: By the late 1960s the war had cost tens of thousands of American lives and huge sums, without breaking North Vietnam's will. Tet, domestic protest and a weakening economy convinced Nixon to seek 'peace with honour' while handing the war to the ARVN.

questions.stem: After 1973, how did the US Congress affect the outcome of the war in Vietnam?
options: It banned new US military action in Indochina and cut aid to South Vietnam
It voted to send US troops back to Vietnam after North Vietnam broke the ceasefire
It increased aid so the ARVN could invade North Vietnam in 1974
It recognised North Vietnam and cut off all contact with Saigon
questions.explanation: The Case-Church Amendment ended funding for US military operations in Indochina from August 1973, and Congress cut military aid to Saigon in 1974. With Nixon gone after Watergate, the USA did not respond when North Vietnam took Phuoc Long province in January 1975.

questions.stem: Why did the ARVN collapse so quickly in the North Vietnamese offensive of 1975?
options: Thieu's ordered retreat from the Central Highlands became a rout, amid aid cuts
US forces withdrew suddenly in March 1975 and left their bases in the highlands undefended
Thieu surrendered the whole army to the NLF to spare Saigon from fighting
China invaded from the north and drew the ARVN's best divisions away
questions.explanation: After Ban Me Thuot fell in March 1975, Thieu ordered a withdrawal from the Central Highlands that turned into chaos. Hue and Da Nang fell within weeks. US combat forces had left in 1973, and aid cuts had left the ARVN short of fuel and ammunition.

questions.stem: Saigon fell to North Vietnamese forces on:
options: 17 April 1975
27 January 1973
2 July 1976
30 April 1975
questions.explanation: North Vietnamese tanks entered Saigon on 30 April 1975, after the last Americans were evacuated by helicopter, and the South surrendered. Phnom Penh fell on 17 April 1975, and Vietnam was formally reunified on 2 July 1976.

questions.stem: Which combination best explains the communist victory in Vietnam?
options: a 1974 agreement under which the USA handed control of the South to Hanoi
unified, determined leadership, outside aid, nationalist appeal and a weak Saigon regime
superior air power, a larger navy and the support of most Western governments
a popular uprising in Saigon in 1973 that the ARVN joined against Thieu
questions.explanation: Hanoi had disciplined leadership willing to accept enormous losses, nationalist legitimacy, sanctuaries in Laos and Cambodia, and Soviet and Chinese aid. South Vietnam's governments were divided, corrupt and dependent on the USA, which withdrew and cut aid.

questions.stem: After 1975, many former South Vietnamese officials and army officers were:
options: given senior posts in the government of the reunified Vietnam
allowed to leave freely for the USA under a United Nations plan
briefly tried and then released under a general amnesty in 1976
held in re-education camps, often for years, without trial
questions.explanation: Hundreds of thousands were sent to re-education camps, many for years of hard labour and political study. Others were moved to New Economic Zones, and many South Vietnamese later fled by sea as 'boat people'.

questions.stem: Which outcome best shows how far southern revolutionaries were sidelined after 1975?
options: Southern NLF leaders took most of the top posts in the government in Hanoi
The NLF forced all North Vietnamese troops to leave the South in late 1975
Northern leaders dominated the new state, and the NLF's own government merged into it in 1976
The NLF ran an independent southern state alongside the North until the 1980s
questions.explanation: The NLF's Provisional Revolutionary Government nominally ruled the South at first, but real power lay with the party in Hanoi. Vietnam was reunified as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam in July 1976, and Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City.
